title: US Military Refueling Planes at Ben Gurion Airport Spark Clash With Israel Over Summer Travel
excerpt: More than 30 American aerial refueling tankers parked at Israel's main airport are threatening to cancel 50,000 flight tickets during peak summer travel season, as renewed US-Iran hostilities keep the aircraft grounded in Tel Aviv.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Over 30 US refueling tankers at Ben Gurion Airport threaten 50,000 summer flight cancellations.
  • Israel's Transportation Minister capped military aircraft at 20, directing others to Air Force bases.
  • US Central Command insists tankers are vital for operations against Iran amid escalating tensions.
  • Major US airlines suspended direct flights to Tel Aviv until at least August, affecting travel plans.

  • The US has more than 30 refueling tankers stationed at Ben Gurion Airport, exceeding the facility's 20-aircraft capacity for military planes and squeezing out commercial flights.
  • Israel's Transportation Minister Miri Regev has ordered a cap of 20 military aircraft and directed remaining planes to Israeli Air Force bases.
  • US Central Command officials have pushed back, calling the tankers a "strategic asset" essential to joint preparations against Iran.
  • Major US carriers — American, Delta, and United — have already suspended direct flights to Tel Aviv through at least August, with Delta and United planning to resume service in September.

Military Buildup Collides With Peak Travel Season

A fleet of American aerial refueling tankers has become the unlikely flashpoint in a dispute between the United States and Israel — not over military strategy, but over airport parking.

The US deployed roughly 75 refuelers and cargo planes to Ben Gurion International Airport ahead of the start of the war with Iran on Feb. 28. While some aircraft were moved out earlier in July, the renewed fighting between Washington and Tehran over the Strait of Hormuz has stalled the drawdown, leaving more than 30 tankers at Israel's busiest airport just as summer travel demand peaks.

The Israel Airports Authority has warned that unless the excess military aircraft are removed, up to 50,000 flight tickets could face cancellation. The airport can accommodate a maximum of 20 military tankers alongside normal commercial operations, and the overflow has forced officials to scramble for gate and tarmac space.

Israel's Transportation Minister Draws a Line

Israeli Transportation Minister Miri Regev responded forcefully on July 14, imposing a hard cap on the number of US military tankers at Ben Gurion.

"Hundreds of thousands of tickets were bought by Israelis to fly and enjoy their summer vacation. We promised that we will enable commercial flights and we will not cancel a single ticket because of American refueling planes."

- Miri Regev, Israeli Transportation Minister

Regev ordered that no additional US refueling tankers be permitted to land at Ben Gurion beyond the agreed 20-plane limit, directing remaining aircraft to Israeli Air Force bases instead.

Washington Fires Back

The announcement drew a sharp reaction from Washington. US officials told Israeli news outlet Ynet that Regev's decision harms US forces' operations during the escalating conflict with Iran. Senior officials at US Central Command (CENTCOM) quickly contacted the Israel Defense Forces and Israel's defense establishment to push back.

A senior Israeli military official, speaking to Ynet, sided with the Americans.

"The American demand is justified. The refueling aircraft are a strategic asset of the United States in the region, and they are an integral part of the joint preparations against Iran."

- Senior Israeli Military Official, via Ynet

CENTCOM spokesman Navy Capt. Tim Hawkins struck a diplomatic tone in a statement, saying the US would "continue working with our Israeli partners to best position US aircraft to support operations."

Broader Context: US-Iran War Escalates

The dispute comes against a backdrop of rapidly escalating hostilities. The US has carried out seven consecutive days of strikes on Iranian military targets, including bridges near the port city of Bandar Abbas on the Strait of Hormuz. Iran has responded by hitting infrastructure in neighboring Kuwait and threatening to shut down oil exports from the region entirely.

More than 20 US Navy warships, including two aircraft carriers — the USS Abraham Lincoln and the USS George H.W. Bush — are patrolling Middle Eastern waters. The aerial refueling tankers at Ben Gurion play a direct role in sustaining these operations, extending the range of fighter jets conducting strikes across Iran.

Diplomatic efforts have not stopped the cycle of escalation. While Qatari mediators visited Tehran last week and Iran dispatched officials to Oman for talks on Strait of Hormuz shipping lanes, a ceasefire agreement reached in June collapsed within weeks.

Impact on Indian Diaspora Travelers

The disruptions add another layer of complexity for Indian travelers transiting through or flying to Israel. Ben Gurion Airport serves as a connection point for several routes, and the ongoing US carrier suspensions — American, Delta, and United have all halted direct service through at least August — are reshaping travel options across the region. Delta plans to resume New York-Tel Aviv flights on Sept. 6, while United targets a Sept. 8 restart, though these timelines remain uncertain given the military situation.

What Comes Next

Israel's tourism sector has already taken severe hits. Visitor numbers dropped 68% in 2024 compared to 2023, falling to just 961,000 arrivals. The continued military presence at Ben Gurion threatens to deepen that decline during what should be the country's strongest travel months.

The standoff exposes a tension at the heart of the US-Israel alliance: Washington needs Ben Gurion's infrastructure to project military power across the region, while Israel needs the same airport to keep its economy and tourism sector alive. With no resolution in sight and the Iran conflict intensifying, both the tankers and the cancellation notices may be staying put.
